Per hundred, and the one idea the whole course is built on.
A percentage tells you how much of something you have, measured against exactly 100 equal parts. It is the everyday shortcut for saying \"out of every hundred\".
The word comes from two words: per and hundred. A percentage always measures against a base of 100.
The percent sign % is the standard way to write a percentage. You will meet it in every competitive exam paper.
Some papers write \"25 per cent\" instead. The meaning is identical.
The part and the whole must refer to the same quantity.
Out of 100 equal parts, how many does 50% stand for?
Out of 100 equal parts, how many does 25% stand for?
What does 100% of a quantity mean?
See a percentage as shaded squares on a hundred-square grid.
A hundred parts are easier to picture than a formula. Split a whole into 100 equal squares and every single square becomes 1%.
Pick a value to shade that many squares.
Each square in the grid is exactly 1% of the whole. Shading a number of squares therefore shows that percentage straight away.
A 100-square grid has exactly 100 parts, so each part can stand for one whole percent. A 10-square grid could only ever show multiples of 10%.
Shaded squares read directly as a percentage.
Convert ½, ¼, ¾ and ⅛ into percentages confidently.
A fraction and a percentage often describe the very same proportion. Moving between the two is a staple of the quantitative section.
Use whichever route is quicker for the fraction in front of you.
If the denominator divides 100, rewrite the fraction with 100 on the bottom and read the numerator as the percentage.
Otherwise divide the numerator by the denominator, then multiply by 100.
Round the result only when the question asks you to.
One third is ⅓, and 100 does not divide by 3 cleanly. Use the divide-then-multiply method there: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333…, then × 100 = 33.33%.
Denominators that divide 100 convert in a single step.
Everything else uses divide by the denominator, then multiply by 100.

A percentage is just a decimal scaled by 100. Because 1 = 100/100, converting between a decimal and a percentage is the same operation as converting between metres and centimetres: you scale by 100. In this lesson you will learn to move the decimal point two places to the right, and you will see why decimals larger than 1 produce percentages larger than 100%.
0.9 -> 0.9 x 100 -> 90 (one digit, so add a zero)

Multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the right. You can move the point itself, or you can write out the shifted number. Either way the answer is the decimal written as a percentage. If there is only one digit after the point, add a zero so you still shift two places.
The rule: shift two places right
Equivalently: move the decimal point two places to the right.

A percentage above 100% is not an error. It simply means the part is larger than the whole being measured. A score of 1.25 as a decimal is 125% of a full mark, and a quantity that grew to 2.5 times its starting size is 250% of what it was. The rule does not change at all; only the size of the number changes.

Moving the decimal point to the left divides by 100 and turns 0.45 into 4.5%. That is the conversion from a percentage to a decimal, done backwards. Remember which direction you are going: to a percentage, the number gets bigger, so the point moves right.
Convert 0.8 into a percentage, then convert 0.035 into a percentage.
To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100, which shifts the point two places right.
Decimals below 1 give percentages below 100%; decimals above 1 give percentages above 100%.
If there is only one digit after the point, add a zero before shifting.
part = (p / 100) x number. Convert first, then multiply.
1% of a number is that number shifted two places left; then multiply by the percentage.
A percentage below 100% must give an answer below the original number.

This is the single most-used percentage operation in aptitude questions. The idea is that a percentage is a fraction of 100, so to take p% of a number you convert p% into a decimal, multiply, and read the result. You will also learn the 1% method, which turns many exam questions into one-step mental arithmetic.
Find a percentage of any number

Write the percentage as a fraction over 100, multiply by the number, then divide by 100. If you can cancel the 100 against something in the question first, the division disappears entirely and you are left with a single multiplication.
Equivalently: part = number x p, then move the decimal point two places left.

One percent is simply one hundredth, so 1% of a number is that number with its decimal point shifted two places left. Once you know 1%, any whole-number percentage is just that multiplied: 6% is six times 1%. This is the fastest route when the percentage is a small whole number, which is exactly what aptitude papers tend to use.

15% of 200 is 30, not 150. The number 150 is 75% of 200, because it is three quarters of it. Always check that your answer is smaller than the original number when the percentage is below 100%; if it is larger, you have multiplied instead of found the part.
Taking the percentage of the wrong number

When you know a part and the percentage it represents, you are being asked for the whole. The operation is the exact inverse of the previous lesson: divide by the percentage instead of multiplying. This is the operation behind every \'is what percent of\' and every \'what was the original\' question.
Work backwards to the original value

Turn the percentage into a decimal, then divide the part by that decimal. Because multiplication and division undo each other, you can always verify the answer by multiplying it back by the same percentage. If the product is not the original part, the arithmetic has gone wrong somewhere.
The method, and the check that proves it
Check it by multiplying the whole by p% and confirming you recover the part.
Rewrite the division as a fraction

If 30 is 15% of the whole, the whole must be larger than 30, because 30 is only a part of it. Any method that produces a number smaller than the given part is wrong. When the percentage is below 100%, dividing always moves you upward.
whole = part / (p / 100). This is the inverse of finding a percentage of a number.
Always multiply back to check the answer.
Cancelling 100 against a factor of p turns the division into a multiplication.
The percentage is always calculated on the starting value.
new value = value x (1 + p/100) for a rise, value x (1 - p/100) for a fall.
A fall and the rise needed to undo it are measured on different bases, so they are not equal.

When a price, a salary or a population rises by a percentage, the percentage is always taken of the starting value. That single rule causes most of the errors in this topic. You will also learn why a 50% fall needs more than a 50% rise to recover, which is the idea that examiners return to again and again.
Increase and decrease, and which base to use

The percentage describes the change, and the change is measured against where the quantity started. So to find how much a 20% rise on 250 adds, calculate 20% of 250 and add that to 250. Calculating 20% of the new value instead would give a different, incorrect answer.
Always take the percentage of the original
change = value x (p / 100) new value = value x (1 + p / 100)

After a 50% fall from 200 you are at 100, which is half the original. To return to 200 you must now gain 100 on a base of 100, which is a 100% rise, not 50%. The loss and the recovery are measured against different bases, so they can never cancel unless both are zero.
Why falls and rises are not symmetric
The recovery is measured on the new base

For a 20% rise on 250, working out 20% of 300 gives 60 and an answer of 310. That is wrong because 300 is the value you are trying to find, not the one you started from. Whenever the question gives you the starting value and the percentage, the starting value is the base.
Applying the percentage to the new value
A quantity falls from 400 by 25%. What is the new value, and what rise on the new value would bring it back to 400?
Each change multiplies the current value, not the original one.
Chain the multipliers, then subtract 1 to get the net decimal change.
A rise of a% then a fall of b% gives a net of a - b - ab/100.

When a price rises 10% and then rises 20%, the second change is not applied to the original price; it is applied to the price after the first change. This lesson gives you a formula that produces the net effect without doing the two-step arithmetic, which is what makes these questions quick rather than laborious.

Each change multiplies the current value by a number slightly above or below 1. A 10% rise multiplies by 1.10, a 20% fall multiplies by 0.80. Chaining the multipliers gives the overall multiplier, and subtracting 1 from it gives the net percentage change.
For a rise of a% then a fall of b%: net % = a - b - (a x b / 100).

A rise of a% followed by a fall of b% gives a net change of a - b - ab/100. The correction term is always subtracted, because the fall was measured on a base that the rise had already enlarged. When a and b are equal, the net is always negative, however large the percentage, which is a useful sanity check.

Adding 10% and 20% gives 30%, but the correct net is 32%. The extra 2% appears because the 20% was applied to 110 rather than to 100, so it carries a little of the first rise with it. Adding is wrong in every case except when one of the changes is zero.
A value of 500 falls by 20% and then rises by 25%. What is the final value, and what is the net change?
If A is p% more than B, then A : B = (100 + p) : 100.
For p% less, the ratio is (100 - p) : 100.
Chain comparisons by expressing everything against the common quantity and multiplying the factors.

Comparison questions usually ask for a ratio, not a raw number: if A is 25% more than B, what is A to B? The method is to put both quantities on the same footing of 100 and read off the ratio. Once you can do that, chained comparisons across three or four quantities become routine.
When is one quantity what percent more than another?

If B is taken as 100, then A being 25% more than B must be 125. The ratio is simply 125 to 100. If A is 20% less than B, then with B as 100, A is 80, giving 80 to 100. Always make the quantity that the percentage is measured from equal to 100.
Put both on a scale of 100
If A is p% more than B, then A : B = (100 + p) : 100
Example: A is 25% more than B
Example: A is 20% less than B

When B is itself a percentage of C, express everything in terms of C and the chain collapses into one multiplication. Take C as 100, build B from it, then build A from B. The result tells you A against C directly, which is usually what the question asks.
A is 50% more than B, and B is 20% less than C. Take C as 100.

If A is 25% more than B, then A is the larger quantity and must be the larger term of the ratio. Writing A : B = 4 : 5 would claim that A is the smaller one, which contradicts the question. As a quick check, the first term should feel bigger whenever the percentage is positive.
If A is 10% more than B, write A : B in lowest whole-number terms.
Percentage points are a subtraction with no base.
Percentage change divides by the earlier value.
Both can be true at once; say which one you mean.

News reports and exam papers both talk about percentages, but two different calculations hide behind the word. A change in percentage points is a plain subtraction. A percentage change is a relative shift measured against the starting value. Mixing them up is one of the most common traps in this subject, so this lesson makes the distinction explicit.
Percentage points and percentage change are different

A percentage point is an absolute unit. Going from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 percentage points, full stop. A percentage change asks by what proportion of the original the value moved: from 20% to 25% is a rise of 5 out of 20, which is 25% relative. The base for a percentage change is the earlier value; there is no base at all in a percentage-point difference.
So both statements are true, and they are not the same fact

Interest rates, tax slabs, poll shares and pass marks are all quoted in percentage points. A loan rate moving from 8% to 10% is described as a rise of 2 percentage points, and that is what the borrower pays, in absolute terms, on a fixed principal. Describing it as a 25% rise would suggest the rate itself grew by a quarter, which is a true but very different fact.
Example: an interest rate from 8% to 10%

If a pass mark rises from 33% to 40%, the marks needed went up by 7 percentage points. But a student who needed 33 out of 100 now needs 40, which is a rise of about 21% in the marks themselves. Reporting only one of the two hides the other.
Saying \'rose by 5%\' when it rose by 5 points
5 percentage points, and 5 / 10 x 100 = 50% relative increase.
A discount moves from 10% to 15%. State both the change in percentage points and the relative percentage change.

A proportion can be written as a fraction, as a decimal, or as a percentage, and all three can appear in the same question. Comparing them is easy once everything is converted to one form. The conversions are: multiply a fraction by 100 to get a percentage, and multiply a decimal by 100 to get a percentage.
Three ways of writing the same quantity

Comparing 33/100 with 1/3 directly tells you nothing, because the denominators differ. Converting both to percentages puts them on a common scale: 33/100 is 33%, and 1/3 is 33.33%. Now the comparison is immediate. When one of the three forms is already a percentage, convert the others to match it.
fraction a/b -> (a / b) x 100 % decimal -> x 100 %
1/2 = 50% and 2/3 of a half is 33.33%, not 50%
A handful of fractions carry most of the weight in these questions, because they have clean percentage equivalents. If you know them by heart you can recognise an answer without computing anything.

0.3 looks bigger than 25% but it is only 30% against 25%, so in this case the decimal does win. Try 0.29 against 2/7: 0.29 is 29%, while 2/7 is about 28.57%, so the decimal wins again. But try 0.4 against 3/8: 0.4 is 40% and 3/8 is 37.5%, and now the fraction looks larger than the decimal if you never converted. Always convert.
0.29 = 29%, and 2/7 is about 28.57%, so 0.29 is larger.
Multiply fractions and decimals by 100 to reach percentages.
Compare only after everything is in the same form.
Clean fractions of 100 are fast but only for clean numbers.
For exactly two changes use a - b - ab/100 after a rise, or b - a - ab/100 after a fall.
Turn comparison questions into ratios on a scale of 100, then reduce.
Never extend a shortcut beyond the case where it is exact.

This lesson collects the techniques that survive exam conditions. Each one is stated with the situation it is good for and, just as importantly, the situation where it does not apply. A shortcut presented without its limits is worse than no shortcut, because it produces a confident wrong answer. None of the methods below are tricks that work only for tidy numbers.
Shortcuts that hold up under pressure

Halves, quarters, fifths and tenths have exact percentage equivalents, so the whole question collapses into one subtraction or division. This is the fastest route when the numbers are friendly. It is not a general method: there is no clean fraction behind 33%, and forcing 33% into \'a third\' gives an answer that is wrong rather than approximate.

For exactly two changes there is a direct formula. A rise of a% followed by a fall of b% nets a - b - ab/100. The mirror case, a fall of a% then a rise of b%, nets b - a - ab/100. Either way the correction term ab/100 is subtracted. This replaces two rounds of multiplying the running value, which is where arithmetic slips usually happen. Use it for exactly two changes; with three changes, multiply the three factors instead.
Shortcut 2: the net formula for two changes
This is the mirror case, so use b - a - ab/100

Convert a \'what percent more or less\' question into a ratio on a scale of 100 and reduce it. This is especially fast when both percentages are whole numbers, because the ratio terms are then whole numbers too and reduction is quick.
Example: a 40% rise in two equal steps

Halving and halving again gives one quarter, so two successive 50% falls leave 25%. That is true. But it does not generalise: two 40% falls leave 36%, not 20%, because the second fall is measured on the already-reduced value. Similarly, a 33% fall is close to one third but is not one third. Always use the exact formula unless the numbers really are clean.
Treating a special case as a general rule
A price falls 40% and then rises 40%. Using 100 as the base, what is the final value and the net change?
